title: Clinical AI: Regulatory breadth leaves autonomy unresolved
desc: Shows medical AI spans multiple tasks and pathways, but does not settle augmentation versus professional substitution.

kps.k: The cluster documents a long regulatory history of medical AI, rather than evidence of professional displacement.
kps.d: The Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Device List supplies device-level records spanning June 1998 to March 2026, with manufacturers, specialties and linked FDA records. Its contribution to the debate is evidence that AI-enabled medical products predate recent generative AI and span decades—not a measured rate of adoption, growth or workforce change.

kps.k: Medical AI covers multiple clinical tasks and specialties, not just diagnostic interpretation.
kps.d: Radiology dominates the supplied records, but its applications include imaging hardware, reconstruction, triage, quantitative analysis, segmentation and treatment planning. Other entries cover cardiac monitoring, endoscopy, ophthalmology, pathology and laboratory medicine. This breadth supports analysing AI at the task and product level; it does not establish equivalent capabilities, clinical benefits or supervision requirements across applications.

kps.k: Product versions and regulatory pathways require separate treatment when interpreting the inventory.
kps.d: AutoContour appears in successive versions from V2 in 2022 through V5 in 2026. Such entries represent dated product records, not independent evidence or necessarily distinct inventions. The list also links to 510(k), De Novo and premarket approval records. Any analysis of product counts or regulatory trends should distinguish versions and pathways rather than describe every entry as the same kind of approval.

kps.k: The inventory leaves the augmentation-versus-substitution debate unresolved.
kps.d: The supplied source advances no competing positions, predictions or recommendations. It provides no performance comparisons, adoption measures, patient-outcome findings or workforce evidence. Assessing whether these products assist or replace clinicians—and whether medical AI offers a useful analogy for legal work—requires separate evidence about deployment, human checking, outcomes and staffing.

vlens.an: The regulatory/professional-body voice represented here supports the proposition, but only at the level of regulatory inventory. The FDA device list substantiates a long history and wide task-level breadth of AI-enabled medical products across radiology and other specialties. It also supports caution in interpreting the records because entries include successive product versions and different regulatory pathways. Crucially, the source does not provide deployment, performance, patient-outcome, supervision or workforce evidence, so it cannot resolve whether these products augment clinicians or substitute for them. There is no source-level disagreement to assess because the curated evidence contains one inventory rather than multiple argumentative sources; the material variation is instead within the records—across dates, specialties, tasks, versions and pathways.

elens.an: The 2026-period source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by documenting the regulatory breadth and long history of AI-enabled medical devices without supplying evidence that resolves clinician augmentation versus substitution. Its inventory spans records from 1998 through March 2026, multiple specialties and varied functions—including imaging, reconstruction, triage, monitoring, pathology and laboratory applications—so it supports task- and product-level analysis rather than a single claim about medical AI capability. It also reinforces the cluster’s methodological caution: successive versions of the same product and different regulatory pathways should not be treated as uniform, independent approvals. There is no substantive internal disagreement because the sole source is an inventory rather than an argumentative account. The material variation lies instead among the listed devices, specialties, functions, versions and pathways. Crucially, the inventory contains no comparative performance, deployment, patient-outcome or workforce evidence from which professional displacement or required levels of human supervision could be inferred. This assessment applies only to the supplied curated source, not to medical-device stakeholders generally.

parents.t: Medical AI device inventories: regulatory breadth does not establish innovation or impact
